title: Learning from Feedback with Tools and Code
summary: Three self-improvement loops that differ only in where the learning signal comes from: ReAct (feedback from environment/tool observations via interleaved thought-action traces), RLEF (feedback from code execution and test pass/fail used as a binary reward in an RL loop), and Constitutional AI (feedback from the model's own critique against a human-written constitution, distilled via SL and then turned into an AI preference model for RL). Recurring mechanisms: grounding unverified model output against an external signal; separating iteration-time feedback from reward-time evaluation to prevent leakage; the hybrid token-level/turn-level credit-assignment problem; and trading helpfulness against harmlessness on a Pareto frontier.

sections.title: Three self-improvement loops: where does the feedback come from?
sections.problem: LLMs are strong at NLP and chat, but to be useful on real-world tasks they must interact with environments, tools, and code, and then learn from that interaction. Test-time compute and robust verification (the previous two lectures) only build part of the picture.
sections.why: A chat-style model has no grounding: it cannot observe the consequences of an action, so it cannot close a feedback loop on its own. The binding question is not whether to self-improve but where the learning signal originates.
sections.how: Study three papers whose loops differ only in feedback source: ReAct (environment/tool observations), RLEF (execution and test feedback for code), and Constitutional AI (model self-critique against human-written principles).
sections.detail:
All three papers answer the same question — where does the learning signal come from? — but differ in the feedback channel:

  • ReAct: feedback = observations returned by tool calls (search results, API responses); reasoning and acting are interleaved in-context.
  • RLEF: feedback = execution/test results of generated code, converted into a binary reward for an RL loop.
  • Constitutional AI: feedback = the model's own critique against a human-written constitution, distilled via supervised learning and then used as an AI preference model for RL.

The unifying claim: once a loop produces enough signal, the model can improve beyond the data it was pretrained on. Modern thinking models already have ReAct-style tool-call traces distilled in, so the loop looks innate rather than hand-engineered.

sections.title: ReAct: reasoning and acting are isolated processes
sections.problem: Models struggle to combine reasoning and acting. Ask a chatbot what the temperature is today and it has no current-events knowledge unless it actually issues a search call, so it confidently hallucinates instead.
sections.why: Humans run a think-act-observe loop (thirsty, walk to kitchen, water is out, decide to go to the store). LLMs historically had no such loop: they had no notion of grounding in the world and could not feed action consequences back into reasoning.
sections.how: ReAct interleaves verbal reasoning traces with actions: prompt the model to think step by step, append that reasoning to the context, then emit an action; the observation feeds the next reasoning step — thought1, act1, observation1, thought2, act2.
sections.detail:
The motivating observation is that reasoning and acting were two disjoint research lines: chain-of-thought reasons over the model's internal state with no external feedback, while WebGPT-style agents learn browser interaction but have no explicit reasoning abstraction. ReAct is the first abstraction that combines them effectively.

  • Each step the model emits either a thought (free-form language that does not affect the environment) or an action (e.g. a search call).
  • The loop runs entirely in language space, so it is cheap to try and easy to inspect.
  • Grounding is the point: a search call fetches an observation the model could not have generated itself, curing the temperature/current-events failure.
  • Today's thinking modes (e.g. Qwen) reproduce this behavior automatically because they were distilled on exactly these traces, so tool calling looks innate.

sections.title: From CoT and WebGPT to interleaved prompting; interpretability
sections.problem: Chain-of-thought gives reasoning but is ungrounded, and action-only agents act but do not reason about what to do. How do you get both in one model, and what does grounding actually buy you?
sections.why: To ground the model you need an external signal, but to decide what to retrieve you need reasoning as an intermediate. Combining internal knowledge with external retrieval via a reasoning step is where the value is.
sections.how: Prompt the model to reason step by step, append the reasoning to the context, then ask which action to take; repeat. A tiny action space (search, lookup, finish) simulates a human interacting with Wikipedia, with no policy training up front.
sections.detail:
CoT intermediate steps may or may not be grounded because they come from the model's internal state and receive no feedback from the outside world. WebGPT-style agents are fine-tuned on browser interaction traces plus human preference data, but learn actions without the reasoning abstraction.

  • Grounding: each observation is external evidence, so hallucination drops relative to CoT.
  • Interpretability: the decision trace is explicit, so humans can audit and trust it — almost like watching the model break a task down step by step.
  • Tasks used: HotpotQA (multi-hop QA), FEVER (fact checking), WebShop (buy products online); all require real-world knowledge and a sequence of tool calls.

Without grounding the model cannot keep making progress; ReAct is the minimal prompting abstraction that supplies it.

sections.title: ReAct as a language-space agent: thoughts vs actions
sections.problem: Interleaving observations and actions implicitly defines a full agent. The principled approach would be to learn a policy over the context and past actions, but that requires a complex and expensive RL loop.
sections.why: A learned policy is expensive, whereas prompting can approximate the same interleaving for free. Thoughts are a language-space abstraction that does not touch the environment; only parsed actions do.
sections.how: Treat the context plus history of actions as state, generate thoughts in language space, then emit an action. Each step informs the next, so the process is sequential; parallel sampling is possible but must be explicitly designed.
sections.detail:
The setup is a full agent: observations about the world plus a set of available actions chosen from the context and action history. ReAct deliberately avoids the policy-learning route by doing everything in the prompting space.

  • Left loop = reasoning traces; right loop = actions on the environment.
  • Interleaving is sequential: thought1, act1, thought2, act2 — each observation informs the next thought, mirroring the human thirsty-to-store example.
  • Reasoning tokens do not act on the environment; only the parsed action does. You can do parallel sampling and similar tricks, but then you must design that process yourself.
  • The abstraction maps naturally onto today's RL-trained thinking models, which already internalized the pattern.

sections.title: Valid-action classification and the PAL frozen-LLM implementation
sections.problem: If the model generates actions, how do you guarantee they are valid, and how does it decide when to reason versus when to act? Open-ended generation can emit malformed or illegal actions.
sections.why: Large or continuous action spaces (e.g. robotics) demand that only valid actions be considered, and demonstrations cannot fit in context, so training a full policy was impractical at the time.
sections.how: Frame action selection as classification over an enumerated valid action subset: given the reasoning, the state of the world, and the valid actions, pick one. Implement with a frozen LLM (the PAL model) plus few-shot exemplars of thought/action/observation triplets.
sections.detail:
Implementation is deliberately lightweight — no policy training required up front. Two decisions matter:

  • Reason or act? Given world state plus prior thinking, emit a reasoning trace or an action.
  • Which action is valid? Instead of open-ended generation, classify over the enumerated valid subset. This gives a more grounded response and was also used in a Google robotics collaboration where a strict state space demanded only valid actions.

The whole loop runs in language space, so it is cheap to try and easy to inspect. A full learned policy over context and action history would require a complex, expensive RL loop; ReAct shows prompting can approximate the same interleaving. Today, RL-trained thinking modes reproduce much of this behavior natively because their traces were distilled from these patterns.

sections.title: Worked example: HotpotQA Apple Remote multi-hop reformulation
sections.problem: The multi-hop question Aside from the Apple Remote, what other device can control the program Apple Remote was originally designed to interact with? defeats standard prompting and full chain-of-thought: both return wrong answers.
sections.why: Answering requires chaining an unverified intermediate fact (Apple Remote to Front Row media center). CoT produces plausible steps but cannot verify them, so the intermediate fact is hallucinated; an action-only agent answers prematurely after the first search.
sections.how: ReAct reasons about what to look up, executes search actions, reads observations, and — critically — when a lookup fails it reformulates the query (Front Row to Front Row software) and reaches the grounded answer.
sections.detail:
Trace from the paper:

  • Standard prompting gives a wrong answer. CoT shows intermediate steps but is still not correct because the facts are ungrounded.
  • Action-only returns that the Apple Remote is a 2005 remote designed to control the Front Row media center, then emits an answer prematurely.
  • ReAct: thought — first find the Apple Remote, then the program it was designed for; act: search[Apple Remote] returns Front Row; act: search[Front Row] fails; thought — try Front Row software; act: search[Front Row software] finds discontinued media-center software; finish with the answer.

The key mechanism is reflection on a failed action: the observation lets the model reformulate its query and recover, which neither CoT (no actions) nor an action-only agent (no reasoning) can do. Failure analysis confirms CoT hallucination is the dominant error mode, while ReAct's grounded observations cut it substantially.

sections.title: Discussion: model self-knowledge, calibration, interleaving, and conflicting evidence
sections.problem: How does the model know what it knows and when to search? Does the action influence the next reasoning step, or are all thoughts emitted first? And what happens when the model and the search result disagree?
sections.why: Models are overconfident and not well calibrated, so a research problem remains open; the practical goal for an application is not knowing whether the model knows but getting it to use the right tools for grounded knowledge. ReAct interleaves in sequence, so each action does inform the next reasoning step.
sections.how: For application design, add guardrails: majority voting / self-consistency and validating the answer before returning it. When evidence conflicts, let the user decide and increase confidence by sampling multiple times or validating. Grounded search hallucination is far more controllable than relying on the internal state.
sections.detail:
Student Q&A clarified several points:

  • Calibration: there are contradictory opinions on whether models know what they know; asked to rate their own confidence they are typically overconfident and not well calibrated. For an application, the goal is not to measure self-knowledge but to route the model to the right tools so its knowledge is grounded.
  • Interleaving: it is thought1, act1, thought2, act2 — genuinely sequential, very much like the human process (thirsty, kitchen, water is out, next decision). Each observation genuinely conditions the next reasoning step.
  • Conflicting observations: if the environment contradicts the model, the user decides; majority voting or a validation step adds confidence and guardrails.
  • Hallucination with search results can be controlled much better than depending on the model's internal state alone.

sections.title: Discussion: KV-cache interleaving patterns and whether reasoning is part of the action space
sections.problem: Do the KV-cache representations of a thought versus an observation show detectable interleaving patterns, given that observations come from the environment and are not generated by the LM? And why are reasoning traces treated as separate from the action space?
sections.why: Observations are produced by the environment, so their hidden-state signature may differ from generated thoughts; the answer to the second question is that language models are trained on language and benefit from reasoning tokens as an intermediate abstraction to emit the right action.
sections.how: The KV-cache question is posed as an open research project using open-source LLMs. Architecturally, reasoning traces live on the left loop and actions on the right loop; if you had true intermediate representations, the explicit reasoning tokens might not even be necessary.
sections.detail:
Two clarifying questions in the ReAct discussion:

  • KV-cache / internal representation: whether the hidden states of thoughts and observations differ in a systematic interleaving pattern is an open question — a suggested class project, workable with open-source LMs. The important structural fact is that observations are injected by the environment, not generated by the model.
  • Action space vs reasoning: the framework does not put reasoning inside the action space. Actions (search, finish) are the right loop; reasoning traces are a separate left loop. The reason for having explicit reasoning tokens is that language models are trained on language and are helped by a reasoning abstraction when choosing the next action. With genuine intermediate representations, those tokens might not matter.

sections.title: ReAct results on HotpotQA and FEVER
sections.problem: Interleaving thought and action looks appealing, but does it beat prompting, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, or action-only agents when those are properly tuned?
sections.why: ReAct adds overhead (extra reasoning tokens and turns), so any benefit must be demonstrated against real baselines rather than an action-only straw man.
sections.how: Compare standard prompting, CoT, CoT-SC, ACT (action-only, two variants), ReAct, and a ReAct-to-CoT-SC fallback on HotpotQA and FEVER with a small action space of search[entity], lookup[string], and finish[answer].
sections.detail:
Tasks: HotpotQA (multi-hop QA over Wikipedia) and FEVER (fact checking); the action space deliberately simulates a human on Wikipedia.

  • Baselines: standard prompting; CoT; CoT-SC (self-consistency, i.e. majority voting); ACT (actions only); ReAct; and a fallback.
  • Findings: ReAct generally beats ACT; it beats CoT on FEVER but not always on HotpotQA; the fallback scheme (CoT-SC when ReAct stalls after N steps, or ReAct when the majority answer occurs less than half the time) beats both individual approaches.
  • Interpretation: the value comes from properly combining model-internal knowledge with external retrieval, using reasoning as the intermediate that decides what to retrieve.
  • Scaling matters: prompting < fine-tuning < RL loop. Fine-tuned ReAct clearly beats prompted ReAct, and an RL loop does even better (covered the following week).

sections.title: Failure modes and the prompting < fine-tuning < RL ladder
sections.problem: Where does ReAct fail, and how much does additional training buy over prompting?
sections.why: Analyzing successful versus failing traces shows which errors dominate. In CoT hallucination is a major failure mode; in ReAct the model has grounded external knowledge and is more trustworthy, so errors are easier to catch and correct with guardrails.
sections.how: Compare error types across methods, then compare prompting against fine-tuning and against an RL loop. Fine-tuned ReAct beats prompted ReAct; an RL loop does even better.
sections.detail:
The failure-mode comparison is the headline: CoT hallucination is the dominant error mode, whereas ReAct retrieves grounded information from an external knowledge base and therefore makes fewer unsupported claims.

  • Grounding makes the model more trustworthy and the decision trace auditable.
  • Prompting vs fine-tuning: once you can fine-tune, ReAct improves clearly; with an RL loop it improves further. The lecture flags the RL loop as next week's material.
  • The takeaway is a ladder — prompting, then supervised fine-tuning, then RL — where each step converts the interleaved trace into a stronger policy.
  • ReAct also performs better across question answering, fact checking, and decision tasks, with lower hallucination and better decision traces.

sections.title: WebShop decision tasks: error cascading and ReAct's limits
sections.problem: In WebShop (buy a product such as a nightstand with drawers from a simulated store), ReAct beats imitation learning and imitation learning + RL, yet still trails human experts — 66.6 versus 82.1 success in the reported setting.
sections.why: These are long multi-step trajectories (search, click, select options, buy), so a wrong early step cascades and corrupts everything downstream. Large action spaces require demonstrations that cannot fit in the context window, and many reasoning steps make inference expensive.
sections.how: Reasoning as an explicit abstraction still raises both the intermediate score and the final task success rate. The comparison is against imitation learning (plain SFT on traces) and imitation learning + RL (SFT plus RL).
sections.detail:
WebShop: purchase a product from a simulated environment; success rate is reaching the task goal, while score reflects intermediate progress.

  • Having the reasoning abstraction with ReAct yields a higher score and higher success rate than imitation learning or imitation + RL.
  • Residual gap cause: errors compound — one bad step propagates through the rest of the trajectory, so success rate is lower than the score.
  • Stated ReAct limitations: huge action spaces need more demonstrations than fit in context, and multiple reasoning steps raise inference cost.
  • Headroom remains large versus human experts (66.6 vs 82.1), motivating the discussion of additional cognitive mechanisms that follows.

sections.title: Class discussion: noisy feedback, reflection, backtracking, and confidence
sections.problem: What happens when the environment feedback is noisy or misleading rather than honest?
sections.why: Misleading feedback can send the agent down repetitive loops, so it cannot blindly trust observations or remain committed to a chain of thought that no longer fits the evidence.
sections.how: Mitigations proposed by the class: add a reflection layer so the agent reasons about what the environment returned; support backtracking when a chain of thought stops making sense; and build better confidence metrics by sampling the same task multiple times and taking the best sample.
sections.detail:
The class exercise surfaced a catalogue of robustness techniques for noisy feedback:

  • Reflection layer: another pass in which the agent reasons about the environment feedback before acting on it, rather than treating it as ground truth.
  • Backtracking: the ability to abandon or rewind a reasoning path when it stops fitting the problem, specifically to escape repetitive loops caused by misleading feedback.
  • Confidence metrics: quantify how much to trust a given piece of feedback; one concrete method is to perform the task several times and take the highest sample, or otherwise estimate model confidence on the environment feedback.

The framing is that robustness is an engineering layer on top of ReAct, not something the base loop provides for free.

sections.title: Class discussion: decomposition, memory, reasoning:action ratio, delegation
sections.problem: If ReAct is only one way to combine reasoning and action, what other cognitive mechanisms should an agent incorporate?
sections.why: Humans condition the mode of thinking on the task — sometimes relying on past experience, sometimes reasoning step by step — and relying on ReAct alone does not always lead to the right place. Some tasks need analysis before any action.
sections.how: The class catalogue: task decomposition before applying ReAct; parallel approaches to thinking; memory of past experience; tuning the reasoning-to-action ratio per task; counteracting overthinking; and building compound systems that benchmark subtasks on different models and delegate by strength.
sections.detail:
Mechanisms proposed and endorsed by the speaker:

  • Task decomposition: if the task is too complex, split it into subtasks before attacking it with ReAct.
  • Memory: reuse past experience rather than re-deriving everything each time.
  • Reasoning-to-action ratio: the ideal ratio is task-dependent; some tasks benefit from much more reasoning before acting, and this could even be trained per task.
  • Overthinking: today's models often produce very long thinking traces even for simple tasks, so there is active work on getting them not to think too much.
  • Compound systems: pick models by parameter count, benchmark subtasks on different models, and delegate tasks to the model that is best at them.

sections.title: RLEF: grounding code LLMs in execution feedback
sections.problem: Coding agents generate code but need a feedback signal to iterate against user intent. Simply showing a base model faulty solutions plus execution output does not, by itself, improve it.
sections.why: Code is uniquely verifiable — you can actually run it and read test pass/fail — so correctness can be turned into a scalar reward. What is missing is a principled loop that feeds per-turn execution feedback back into generation and uses the final result to update the policy.
sections.how: RLEF is an end-to-end RL fine-tuning framework: action = generated code, observation = execution feedback (running tests and collecting pass/fail output), reward = binary from whether tests pass, optimized with PPO.
sections.detail:
RLEF (RL with Execution Feedback) was among the first papers to show that execution feedback markedly improves coding LLMs. It maps the agent loop directly onto RL:

  • Action = the generated code solution.
  • Observation = execution feedback — actually running tests and collecting the pass/fail output.
  • Reward = binary, from whether tests pass.

Motivation: a majority of the class already uses Claude Code, and much engineering work has been delegated to these agents. The critical requirement is understanding user intent and getting feedback on the generated code so the agent can iterate. The paper's two innovations are the two-tier test strategy and the hybrid token-level / turn-level policy.

sections.title: RLEF's iterative loop: exploitation, public-test iteration, private-test reward
sections.problem: How is the generation cycle structured, and where exactly does the learning signal enter?
sections.why: The loop has two phases: the model exploits its current policy through inference-time feedback, then the policy is updated from execution results, which is what enables continuous self-improvement.
sections.how: A natural-language problem description is given; the model generates a solution; it is evaluated on public tests; if it fails, the execution feedback is appended and the model retries until it passes or hits a turn limit. Passing solutions go to a private test set, whose verdict determines the reward used in the PPO update.
sections.detail:
Concretely, on a palindrome-substring problem the first attempt fails the public tests with an execution timeout — a very common issue. After receiving that feedback the model produces an optimized solution that passes the public tests.

  • Left / exploitation phase: exploit the current policy through inference-time feedback loops.
  • Right / policy update: update the policy from execution results, enabling continuous self-improvement.
  • Only solutions that clear the public tests advance to the private evaluation and policy update.
  • The feedback is real execution (a Python test function), not the model's self-assessment.

This separation of iteration-time feedback from reward-time evaluation is the core of the self-improvement loop.

sections.title: Two-tier test strategy: preventing reward leakage and memorization
sections.problem: If the tests supplying iteration feedback are the same tests that determine the reward, the model can learn to memorize test outputs instead of learning to program, destroying generalization.
sections.why: This is reward-signal leakage: the feedback the model conditions on and the target it is graded on must be disjoint, or the objective is trivially satisfiable by memorization. Real competition design works the same way — public sample tests for iteration, hidden system tests for the verdict (CodeContests).
sections.how: Split the suite into public tests (a small subset visible during generation, giving immediate fine-grained feedback for faster iteration) and private tests (hidden entirely, used only to score the final solution and compute the reward).
sections.detail:
Public tests provide immediate feedback that guides better solution development; because they are only a small subset, iteration is fast. Private tests stay completely hidden during generation and determine the PPO reward.

  • If the feedback tests equal the reward tests, the model can simply memorize test outputs; keeping reward tests hidden forces genuine program synthesis.
  • Feedback is fed back to the LM as explicit execution output — here is the output you generated and here is the feedback you got.
  • Q&A clarified that the split is a design choice over a fixed test set; for CodeContests you keep some tests public for inference-time feedback and some to train.
  • The speaker called this a very useful innovation in the self-improvement loop; hard problems may additionally need richer error traces.

sections.title: Hybrid token-level / turn-level policy optimization
sections.problem: In language-space RL the policy emits code one token at a time, but execution feedback for a solution only exists after the whole response is generated. Which granularity does the advantage use?
sections.why: Reward arrives at the end of the turn, so per-token credit assignment is ill-defined without a value estimate for every token, yet per-token control over generation is exactly what makes code synthesis tractable.
sections.how: Use a hybrid objective: token-level generation and control combined with a turn-level value function. The reward is computed over the entire response using the last token of the prompt, and a single advantage value is broadcast to all tokens in that turn.
sections.detail:
The mismatch between token-level generation and turn-level reward is resolved by a hybrid policy objective:

  • Token-level: the policy emits code token by token, giving fine-grained control over generation.
  • Turn-level: the value function scores the entire response using only the last token, so one advantage value is shared by all tokens in the turn.

The speaker maps this to PPO and notes the turn-level broadcast is closer to GRPO/GSPO-style sequence-level rewards than to strict per-token credit assignment. The trade-off is explicit: a sequence-level advantage is simple, stable, and cheap but blurs which token caused pass/fail. Per-token or per-step rewards could localize credit better — the unresolved process reward model vs outcome reward model debate, which may need different answers per domain and benchmark. Remaining design choices: how many turns to allow, and whether to provide richer error traces or suggestions beyond raw test output.

sections.title: Q&A: where public tests come from, and what a failed test means
sections.problem: Where do the public tests come from on the very first turn, and who or what decides that a test failed?
sections.why: The evaluation must be an actual execution, not the model's self-assessment, and the user can supply arbitrary problem descriptions, so the loop has to be designed around a fixed test set.
sections.how: Keep one set of tests as public and another as private; for CodeContests you keep a subset public for inference-time feedback and a subset for training. Failing means the generated solution is incorrect; the raw test output is appended to the LM as explicit execution feedback before the next attempt.
sections.detail:
Student questions and answers:

  • Source of public tests: you hold out a set of tests as public and another as private. This is designed for the automatic loop — for example with CodeContests, design the auto loop so the model can improve, keeping some tests for inference-time feedback and some to train on.
  • Meaning of failure: a failing test says the generated solution is not correct. The test output is fed to the model — you failed — and that output is the execution feedback that goes back into the LM.
  • Who evaluates: it is an actual running test, e.g. a simple Python function, not a model judgment. In the homework the analogous exercise is on math, identifying the error in a generated solution rather than executing code.

sections.title: RLEF results: solve rate and targeted error repair
sections.problem: Does execution-feedback RL actually raise code solve rates, and does training on competitive programming transfer to other coding benchmarks?
sections.why: The base model does not profit from merely seeing faulty solutions and execution feedback. What helps is that feedback is shown every turn, so the model learns where the error is and makes targeted repairs instead of random edits — and this generalizes.
sections.how: Train on CodeContests with per-turn execution feedback and evaluate solve rate over a sampling budget on validation and test splits; then analyze error counts per turn and the number of code changes.
sections.detail:
Results on Llama 3.1 trained on CodeContests:

  • Solve rate rises substantially with RLEF on both validation and test. Solve-rate 10@K means passing at least one of 10 generated solutions; the x-axis (sampling budget) is log-scaled, so gains are real but front-loaded.
  • Error analysis across turns 1, 2, 3 shows RLEF yields fewer wrong outputs and increasingly targeted edits. Without the iteration loop the model makes incorrect edits rather than repairs.
  • Mechanism: leverage both higher sample diversity and the per-turn error localization that lets the model repair rather than regenerate.
  • Failures shift toward timeout errors when the solution never becomes correct.
  • Takeaway: execution feedback improves code generation and generalizes to other benchmarks in the code-generation realm.

sections.title: RLEF Q&A: is binary reward enough? generalization and SFT vs RL
sections.problem: Is a binary reward sufficient to drive improvement, especially for harder problems? Does the method encourage first-turn correctness? Does RL beat supervised fine-tuning?
sections.why: CodeContests problems are small and simple, so binary feedback was enough; harder problems likely need richer error traces or metadata to debug efficiently. SFT on reasoning traces captures in-domain gains, but RL is able to solve slightly newer problems and thus generalizes more.
sections.how: Discussion of reward design at the final solution versus per-step rewards, and whether the model gets enough chances to self-correct before the private-test evaluation.
sections.detail:
Key exchanges:

  • Binary sufficiency: plausible that for more complex problems you would also need error traces or other metadata, not just pass/fail. This was flagged as a good project idea.
  • First-turn correctness: the method does not force it; the model may take multiple turns, and for simple enough problems can often become correct. There is inference-time feedback plus the public-test gate before PPO, so the model gets a few chances to correct itself.
  • Generalization: contest problems are harder than typical human-level coding, which may be why RLEF generalizes. SFT on reasoning traces still yields in-domain gains (same loss function), but RL shows a bit more generalization to newer/out-of-domain problems.
  • Process vs outcome: the debate is not fully solved; different domains and benchmarks may need different choices. Residual failures are mostly timeout errors when the solution is still not correct, and much of this is domain specific.

sections.title: Long-context repos: retrieval and summarization before patching (SWE-bench, CodeMonkey)
sections.problem: What do you do when the codebase does not fit in the context window, as in real-repo engineering tasks?
sections.why: You cannot feed the whole repository to the model. You must first decide what information is needed, retrieve it, and only then produce a patch and test it — so retrieval and summarization are prerequisites for the test-pass step.
sections.how: Use ReAct-style behavior: think about what information is needed, use search tools, and continue until enough information is gathered. Condense or summarize each document so summaries fit in context; use graph factorization plus similarity (RAG); then generate the code patch and check whether the test passes.
sections.detail:
The class proposed and the speaker endorsed several approaches:

  • Search/retrieval first: think about what is needed, search, and only move on when enough information is available — exactly the previous paper's pattern.
  • Summarization: condense the code of each document into a short summary so the summaries together fit in context.
  • RAG / representation: graph-factorize the code and retrieve by similarity, then iterate; in the loop, verify whether enough information was gathered and if not retrieve again.

This is what actually runs inside Claude Code: search for the relevant code, apply the edit, then test. One benchmark targeting this is SWE-bench; the speaker notes one slide was skipped and the takeaway is that execution feedback generalizes across coding benchmarks. CodeMonkey (from Aalya's lab) targets very similar ideas.

sections.title: Constitutional AI: replacing human labels with a written constitution
sections.problem: RLHF needs tens of thousands of human preference labels — slow, tedious, and unscalable — yet base models can produce harmful outputs, and we want models that are both helpful and harmless.
sections.why: Human feedback is the bottleneck. But models are now good at instruction following, so you can ask whether an output exhibits a behavior and ask for a rewrite — turning human-written rules into a scalable feedback source with humans in the loop only to write the rules.
sections.how: Write a constitution of 16 human-written principles. For each output issue a critique request (is it harmful/unethical, gender-biased, inappropriate for children?) and a revision request (remove that content). Fine-tune on the self-critique/revision traces (supervised stage), then train an AI preference model on those responses plus the constitution and RL the LLM (RLAIF).
sections.detail:
RLHF collects human preferences (is the output correct, useful, specific enough?) to build a reward model; larger models clearly benefit more from RLHF than from plain fine-tuning. Constitutional AI replaces the labels with principles.

  • The constitution is 16 principles defining desired behavior, written by humans, used as the seed for the self-improvement loop.
  • Each principle becomes a prompt that elicits whether the model is following the constitution, critiques the output, and asks for a revision.
  • Revising requires two capabilities: detecting the behavior in text, and following the rewrite instruction. Both are emergent instruction-following skills the paper exploits.
  • Example critiques in the paper cover harm/unethical content, gender bias, and content inappropriate for children, each paired with a revision request.

sections.title: CAI supervised stage: the helpfulness / harmlessness trade-off
sections.problem: Does supervised learning on self-revisions actually improve harmlessness without destroying helpfulness?
sections.why: Pushing the model toward a fixed set of principles can make it less helpful, but the paper's claim is that helpfulness plus harmlessness improves monotonically overall. There is no explicit feedback signal — only a reshaped output distribution biased toward the revised responses, which holds as long as fine-tuning is small relative to pretraining.
sections.how: Fine-tune on the critique/revision traces and measure helpfulness and harmlessness as revisions increase.
sections.detail:
The mechanism is deliberately simple: the model generates responses, critiques them against the constitution, revises them, and is fine-tuned on the revised traces. Student Q&A drew out the key subtlety:

  • This stage simply reinforces the likelihood of the revised generations — it biases the distribution toward constitutional responses rather than optimizing an explicit reward.
  • Because the fine-tuning is much smaller than pretraining, the model does not lose its initial capabilities, but its output distribution starts to shift.
  • With increasing revisions, harmlessness improves and helpfulness declines under pure supervised learning, yet the combined helpfulness-plus-harmlessness metric improves monotonically.
  • The speaker framed this as a general pattern used in many later pipelines, not unique to Constitutional AI.

sections.title: CAI RL stage and the constitution-amendment problem
sections.problem: How is the preference model trained and used, and what happens when the constitution must be amended?
sections.why: A preference model trained on AI critiques substitutes for human preference labels (RLAIF). But updating or removing rules is a continual-learning / unlearning problem, and there is no proven way to make a model forget a rule.
sections.how: Train a preference model on the stage-1 responses plus the constitution, then RL-fine-tune the LLM to maximize it, so the model responds in the most thoughtful, respectful, and cordial way. Amendments are handled because RLAIF is a late post-training stage (roughly 5% of compute) that is rerun frequently.
sections.detail:
Stage 2 replaces the RLHF loop: instead of tens of thousands of human labels, a preference model trained with the constitution provides the reward signal.

  • The preference model is trained separately from the constitution and then used to fine-tune the LLM.
  • Validation: when training the preference model you keep a test/validation set and check agreement with human scores, but it is not scaled to 10,000 labels — it works compositionally from the principles.
  • Amendments: post-training is a small percentage of total compute and is refreshed often, so a changed constitution can be reapplied. However, making the model completely remove old rules is unsolved; interpretability-based cancellation is proposed but not proven.
  • The speaker flagged continual learning as an open research problem.

sections.title: CAI results: the helpfulness / harmlessness Pareto frontier
sections.problem: Where on the helpfulness/harmlessness plane does constitutional RL land relative to human-feedback RLHF?
sections.why: Helpfulness and harmlessness trade off inversely — making a model more harmless can hurt the helpful axis — so the real objective is the Pareto frontier between the two, not a single axis.
sections.how: Plot harmlessness ELO on the y-axis against helpfulness ELO on the x-axis and compare: raw base model, helpful-only RLHF, helpful-plus-harmless RLHF, constitutional supervised learning, constitutional RL, and constitutional RL with chain-of-thought. Also sweep the number of training sequences on separate helpfulness-ELO and harmlessness-ELO axes.
sections.detail:
Ordering on the helpfulness/harmlessness plane:

  • Raw pretrained base model is lowest; helpful-only RLHF pushes toward higher helpfulness; helpful-plus-harmless RLHF does better on both.
  • Constitutional supervised learning alone is still below RLHF.
  • Constitutional RL with chain-of-thought reaches the best Pareto frontier — the headline result.
  • Replacing human preferences with AI feedback still yields a model that is roughly equally helpful (maybe slightly less) but much more harmless, which is where Claude models were historically strong.
  • Because harmlessness rises at the cost of helpfulness, the practical objective is to find the right balance — the frontier — rather than maximize one axis.
  • The pattern generalizes to any conflicting instruction-following objective, not just helpfulness vs harmlessness.

sections.title: Follow-on work: RLAIF vs RLHF, Self-Refine, consensus critique
sections.problem: Is self-critique a reliable feedback signal, and what research followed Constitutional AI?
sections.why: Getting a model to critique itself is harder than it looks because models are overconfident and not well calibrated. A consensus of models often critiques better than a single self-critique.
sections.how: Follow-ons: a paper comparing RLAIF with RLHF; Self-Refine, which does iterative refinement with self-feedback; and work that teaches models self-correction with reinforcement learning. The speaker frames this as an active area beyond the helpfulness/harmlessness paradigm and a source of project ideas.
sections.detail:
These follow-ons extend the core idea that a model can generate its own feedback, but refine how reliable that feedback is:

  • RLAIF vs RLHF: direct comparison of AI feedback against human feedback as the preference source.
  • Self-Refine: iterative refinement driven by self-feedback, closely related to the critique/revision stage.
  • Self-correction RL: training models to self-correct rather than relying on a fixed constitutional critique.
  • Consensus critique: because a model can be overconfident in what it does not know, aggregating critiques across several models can work better than isolated self-critique.

The unifying takeaway from all three papers: build a feedback loop on top of the model, and when the loop carries enough signal, the model improves beyond the data it was trained on.

sections.title: Recap: three feedback channels
sections.problem: What is the unifying lesson across ReAct, RLEF, and Constitutional AI?
sections.why: When a feedback loop carries enough signal, the model has a way to improve beyond the data it was trained on. The three papers are worked examples of that principle with different feedback sources.
sections.how: Recap the three channels: ReAct (act in the real world, combine environment feedback with reasoning to ground answers and decisions), RLEF (execution/test feedback to iteratively generate correct code, reducing the compute budget to reach state of the art on competitive programming), and Constitutional AI (self-critique against human-written rules, or any rule set whose compliance can be checked).
sections.detail:
Summary of what was covered:

  • ReAct: get the model to act and combine the resulting observations with reasoning, so it is grounded and can answer questions, check facts, and act as a decision maker in games or browser agents. A key benefit of doing it in language space is that decision traces are extremely interpretable. Tool calling is now innate in many out-of-the-box models, but ReAct is the building block.
  • RLEF: coding agents need execution feedback, best obtained from unit tests, to iteratively produce correct code; this reduces the budget needed to reach state-of-the-art competitive-programming performance.
  • Constitutional AI: use a constitution of human-written principles to generate self-improvement feedback, generalizable to any rule set where compliance can be evaluated.

sections.title: Closing discussion: cognitive science, agent transfer, and the boundaries of the approach
sections.problem: Are there systematic ways to import cognitive/behavioral science into LLMs? Do these techniques transfer to agents? Does ReAct's handcrafted framework become obsolete under RL? Is context simply the state? Can harmful outputs be restricted directly?
sections.why: We still use parallels from how humans solve problems because reasoning-space search is not automated for open-ended tasks. The deeper question is whether reasoning-space search can be defined and automated; for finance or legal agents the workflow is inherently domain specific.
sections.how: Speaker answers: closed-source models hill-climb without naming the reasoning space; ReAct defines the sequence or workflow (reason, act, reason, act), and generalizing it to an agent is domain specific. Context is the state in prompting. Reward can shape token generation, but the workflow that accomplishes the task still matters. Harmful-output restriction happens partly, but since models are trained on internet data, no amount of restriction removes all of it, and data filtering plays a large role.
sections.detail:
Final Q&A themes:

  • Cognitive science: we use human-style heuristics (think step by step, decompose, analyze, run parallel loops) because the reasoning space is not well defined. If a well-defined search space exists — as in games with limited actions — you can define and automate the search; for open-ended experience with real tools you must collect observations and use them.
  • Agents: this is a fundamental building block; an agent adds interconnected models, memory, and sessions, but how an LLM responds in a certain way remains the foundation.
  • ReAct under RL: partly yes, partly no. If you can define the search space, RL can handle it; but for a finance or legal agent the required workflow is domain specific, so some handcrafted structure persists.
  • Formalism: the context C-sub-t is treated as the state — in prompting, state literally is what is in the context.
  • Restriction: some filtering happens, but models trained on the internet cannot be fully scrubbed.
